summary: Teaches ages 6–7 to add three one-digit numbers efficiently by scanning for a pair that makes ten (or a double), adding that pair first, then adding on the third number — e.g. 5 + 7 + 3 → 7 + 3 = 10, then 5 + 10 = 15. The objective is the strategic habit of scanning and reordering (supported by commutativity/associativity and fluent bonds to 10), not merely getting a correct total. Includes a hands-on manipulative core, fluency/strategy-choice practice, a narration conversation, and a worked anchor, with each scaffold's role made explicit. Interactive and efficacy details are proposed, not validated.
misconceptions: Always adding left-to-right and never scanning for a make-ten pair.
Not recognising a pair that makes ten because bonds to 10 aren't fluent.
Losing or double-counting the third addend after making ten.
Thinking the numbers must be added in the written order.
Miscounting when crossing ten while adding the third number by ones.

activities.title: Drag a pair to make ten on the ten-frame
steps: Start with three movable number tiles above a ten-frame, e.g. 5, 7 and 3.
Scan the three tiles and decide which two you would add first: a pair that makes exactly ten, or, if there is no such pair, a double.
Drag two tiles together; if they make ten the frame fills completely and leaves a simpler 'ten and a bit' (here 5 + 10).
Deliberately try a less useful pairing first (e.g. 5 + 7 = 12) and notice the frame does not land on a clean ten, then find the better pair — it still gives a correct total, just by a slower route.
Repeat with triples that reward a make-ten pair, and with at least one triple that rewards a double instead.
Add the remaining third tile on last and read the running total.
activities.insight: Spotting the pair that makes ten (or a double) first turns an awkward three-number sum into an easier one: a make-ten pair leaves 'ten and a bit', and a double gives a known fact to add on to. The written order is not fixed, you are free to reorder, and any ordering still gives the same total.

activities.title: Which pair makes it easiest? — fluency and strategy choice
steps: Given a triple such as 5 + 7 + 3, choose which two numbers you would add first and say why.
Complete fill-in-the-blank totals for a set of triples, each containing a make-ten pair that is not the first two written.
Do a short, light timed set of spotting make-ten pairs to build quick recall of bonds to 10.
For each item, state the pair chosen and the leftover number before giving the total.
activities.insight: Fluent recall of bonds to 10 lets you spot the useful pair quickly; deliberately choosing a make-ten pair can make the addition quicker and less error-prone than always adding left-to-right.

activities.title: Narrate the pair you chose
steps: A tutor poses triples such as 5 + 7 + 3, 8 + 2 + 6 and 4 + 9 + 1.
For each, work out the total and say which two numbers you added first and why that choice helps.
Answer follow-ups: 'Is there a pair here that makes exactly ten?', 'Would you get the same total in a different order?', 'For 4 + 9 + 1, which pair makes ten and which number is left to add on?'
activities.insight: Explaining the chosen pair makes the scanning strategy explicit and surfaces whether the child is truly scanning or just adding in written order.

activities.title: Worked anchor: see the make-ten pair highlighted
steps: Study a worked triple, e.g. 5 + 7 + 3, with the 7 + 3 pair highlighted as it makes ten.
Follow the two steps: pair to ten (7 + 3 = 10), then add the third (5 + 10 = 15).
Describe in your own words how the pair was chosen before moving to practice items.
activities.insight: A clear model of the scan-pair-add sequence gives a reference point for the strategy before independent practice.

checkQuestion: Work these out, and each time tell me which two numbers you added first: 5 + 7 + 3; 8 + 2 + 6; 4 + 9 + 1.
checkAnswer: 15, 16, 14. Watch for the child spotting and adding the make-ten pair first (7+3, then 8+2, then 9+1) and adding the remaining number on — rather than ploughing left-to-right.
